title: How Long Will $1 Million Last in Retirement? Exact Years
metaDescription: How long will $1 million last in retirement? See exact years by monthly spending and real return, the 30-year spending ceiling and when it never runs out.
h1: How Long Will $1 Million Last in Retirement?
cardBlurb: Modeled years a $1,000,000 balance lasts at six monthly spending levels and four real returns, plus the spending ceiling for 20 to 35 years.
introText: A $1,000,000 balance lasts anywhere from about 10 years to more than 45 years depending on monthly spending and the real rate of return. At a flat withdrawal of $4,000 a month, $1,000,000 lasts about 20.8 years at a 0% real return, 27 years at a 2% real return, and 44.9 years at a 4% real return. At $3,333.33 a month or less with a 4% real return, the principal never reaches zero in the mathematical model.

sections.heading: How Long $1,000,000 Lasts at Different Monthly Spending Levels
sections.body:
Your monthly withdrawal rate determines how many years your savings last. At ModernWallet, we ran the numbers through the same investment engine as our [withdrawal calculator](/investing/withdrawal-calculator/) at four real returns and six monthly spending levels to see how many years each lasts. Using flat withdrawals in today's dollars, we mapped scenarios from zero growth up to a 5% real annual return. Withdrawals are taken at the end of each month, and the annual real return is divided by 12.

| Monthly Spending | 0% Real Return | 2% Real Return | 4% Real Return | 5% Real Return |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| $3,000 | 27.8 years | 40.6 years | Does not run out | Does not run out |
| $3,333.33 | 25.1 years | 34.8 years | Does not run out | Does not run out |
| $4,000 | 20.8 years | 27.0 years | 44.9 years | Does not run out |
| $5,000 | 16.7 years | 20.3 years | 27.6 years | 35.9 years |
| $6,000 | 13.9 years | 16.3 years | 20.3 years | 23.8 years |
| $8,000 | 10.4 years | 11.8 years | 13.5 years | 14.8 years |

Inputs and conventions are stated here; entering the real return as the return in the withdrawal calculator with a flat withdrawal gives the same rows, though the reader should check the inputs shown on that calculator. In these modeled results, "does not run out" means the monthly withdrawal is equal to or less than the monthly investment return, so the portfolio principal never depletes.

A retiree spending $3,000 a month with no investment growth will deplete the balance in 27.8 years. That same $3,000 monthly spend extends to 40.6 years at a 2% real return. Once the real return reaches 4%, a $3,000 monthly draw requires less than the annual portfolio gain, leaving the starting $1,000,000 intact over any retirement horizon.

Moving your draw to $5,000 a month shortens the timeline. At 0% real return, the money lasts 16.7 years. At a 2% real return, it lasts 20.3 years. It reaches 27.6 years at 4% and 35.9 years at 5%. When spending reaches $8,000 per month, even a 5% real return keeps the portfolio alive for only 14.8 years.

sections.heading: What the Real Return Assumption Means
sections.body:
A real return is the portfolio return that remains after accounting for inflation.

As an example of the arithmetic, consider a 7% nominal portfolio return alongside 3% inflation. The real return is not simply 4%. The exact calculation divides the nominal factor by the inflation factor (1.07 / 1.03 - 1 = 0.0388), resulting in an actual real return of about 3.9%. Our calculations do not forecast future asset returns or economic inflation rates; they model fixed real return benchmarks.

Holding monthly withdrawals flat in today's dollars means the dollar amount pulled from accounts must increase each year to match the rising cost of goods. By using real returns, the model reflects a retiree maintaining the exact same purchasing power over 20, 30, or 40 years. This table holds withdrawals flat in today's dollars so payouts adjust for inflation, whereas a calculator that holds nominal withdrawals flat will show different timelines.

For instance, withdrawing $4,000 a month with a 0% real return leaves you with 20.8 years of income. Increasing that net real yield to 2% adds more than six full years of income, bringing portfolio longevity to 27 years. Increasing it to 4% yields 44.9 years of support. That four-point difference in real return more than doubles the lifespan of your savings. Longevity depends only on the ratio of monthly spending to the starting balance: $2,000,000 at $8,000 a month lasts the same 20.8, 27, and 44.9 years as $1,000,000 at $4,000, and $2,000,000 at $10,000 matches the $5,000 row.

sections.heading: How Much You Can Spend for 20, 25, 30, and 35 Years
sections.body:
Living to 90 means 35 years of withdrawals from age 55, 30 years from age 60, and 25 years from age 65.

To find the maximum monthly spending $1,000,000 supports across fixed retirement horizons, our investment engine calculated the highest flat monthly draw in today's dollars that empties the balance to zero at the end of each period.

| Horizon | 0% Real Return | 2% Real Return | 4% Real Return | 5% Real Return |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 20 Years | $4,166.67 / mo | $5,058.83 / mo | $6,059.80 / mo | $6,599.56 / mo |
| 25 Years (Retire at 65 to 90) | $3,333.33 / mo | $4,238.54 / mo | $5,278.37 / mo | $5,845.90 / mo |
| 30 Years (Retire at 60 to 90) | $2,777.78 / mo | $3,696.19 / mo | $4,774.15 / mo | $5,368.22 / mo |
| 35 Years (Retire at 55 to 90) | $2,380.95 / mo | $3,312.63 / mo | $4,427.75 / mo | $5,046.88 / mo |

For a retiree stepping away at age 65 who wants funds to last until age 90 (25 years), zero real growth permits spending $3,333.33 a month. Earning a 2% real return increases that monthly draw to $4,238.54. A 4% real return pushes the the highest flat monthly withdrawal that uses the balance up in 25 years to $5,278.37.

For an earlier retiree at age 60 planning for 30 years, zero investment growth allows a monthly draw of $2,777.78. A 2% real return provides $3,696.19 per month, while a 4% real return delivers $4,774.15. If planning begins at age 55 across a 35-year window, the monthly allowance ranges from $2,380.95 at 0% real return up to $4,427.75 at 4% real return. To see how these spending caps compare with smaller balances, see our breakdown on [how long will 150k last in retirement](/guides/how-long-will-150k-last-in-retirement/).

sections.heading: Living on the Return Alone
sections.body:
Retirees who want to preserve their initial $1,000,000 nest egg can choose to live strictly on the portfolio's real yield. By withdrawing an amount equal to the monthly real return, the underlying balance remains at $1,000,000 in constant purchasing power indefinitely.

Interest-only income on $1,000,000 produces predictable monthly amounts across real return baselines:

- 2% real return: $20,000 a year, equal to $1,666.67 a month.
- 3% real return: $30,000 a year, equal to $2,500.00 a month.
- 4% real return: $40,000 a year, equal to $3,333.33 a month.
- 5% real return: $50,000 a year, equal to $4,166.67 a month.

The benchmark 4% withdrawal rate traces back to the research published by Cooley, Hubbard and Walz in the AAII Journal, widely known as the [Trinity Study](https://www.aaii.com/journal/article/retirement-savings-choosing-a-withdrawal-rate-that-is-sustainable). The authors analyzed historical market cycles. They reported that withdrawing 4% of a portfolio's initial balance in year one, followed by annual inflation adjustments, lasted 30 years in most historical periods for portfolios weighted toward equities.

On a $1,000,000 balance, the 4% rule generates an initial annual income of $40,000, or $3,333.33 a month. The Trinity Study reported a historical result. It is not a guarantee. You can read more about broad portfolio structures in our guide on [retirement withdrawal strategies](/guides/retirement-withdrawal-strategies/) and our review of [how to retire with 1 million](/guides/how-to-retire-with-1-million/).

sections.heading: What Pushes the Number Up or Down
sections.body:
The mathematical models above isolate investment returns and flat monthly spending, but actual retirement outcomes depend on several financial variables.

Guaranteed external income extends how long your savings last. Every dollar received from Social Security or a traditional pension reduces the amount you must pull from your investment portfolio. Use our [Social Security retirement calculator](/retirement/social-security-retirement-calculator/) to project your benefit and evaluate your net portfolio draw.

Taxes and portfolio account types also alter the lifespan of your funds. Withdrawals from pre-tax accounts, such as traditional 401(k) (a workplace retirement plan) and individual retirement account (IRA) plans, are subject to ordinary income taxes. Taxes increase the gross distribution needed for everyday spending. That higher gross draw speeds up portfolio depletion.

Sequence-of-returns risk represents another factor that fixed-rate models do not capture. In the real world, market returns do not arrive in identical annual increments. A run of poor returns early in retirement can empty a balance sooner than a fixed average return shows (sequence-of-returns risk). Finally, healthcare costs, long-term care needs, and shifting spending patterns are not in the model. You can map out your total household cash flow across different asset types with our [retirement income calculator](/retirement/retirement-income-calculator/).

This analysis does not fit someone who needs $5,000 or more a month from the portfolio alone over 30 years at a 4% real return or lower. At $5,000 a month, $1,000,000 lasts 16.7 to 35.9 years depending on the real return (0%, 2%, 4%, or 5%), so check that row in the table. Other income lowers the draw, which you can check with our [Social Security retirement calculator](/retirement/social-security-retirement-calculator/). Readers expecting returns below inflation should read the 0% column. The projected longevity figures will change whenever actual returns drop, tax rates shift, or expenses grow faster than inflation.

sections.heading: Our Takeaway
sections.body:
Based on our internal modeling, $1,000,000 lasts about 10 to more than 45 years depending on monthly spending and the real return. For a 30-year retirement spanning age 60 to age 90, $1,000,000 supports a flat monthly draw of about $2,780 with no growth, about $3,700 at a 2% real return, and about $4,770 at a 4% real return. Withdrawing more than those amounts will cause the portfolio balance to deplete before reaching year 30.

This nest egg works well for a retiree whose other guaranteed income sources, including Social Security and pensions, cover remaining household overhead. It does not fit a reader who needs $5,000 or more a month from the portfolio alone over three decades at a 4% real return or lower, or who expects portfolio returns to fall below inflation rates.

Our modeling assumes constant withdrawals in today's dollars, but your actual outcome will shift based on external income, early sequence-of-returns losses, taxes owed on retirement account withdrawals, and lifestyle costs that outpace inflation. To verify how long your portfolio will last under your own numbers, run your planned spending through our [withdrawal calculator](/investing/withdrawal-calculator/) and review your baseline with a certified financial planner or certified public accountant (CPA).

faqs.question: What is a safe withdrawal rate in retirement?
faqs.answer: A widely recognized baseline is 4% of your initial portfolio value in year one, adjusted upward for inflation in subsequent years. Originating from the Trinity Study by Cooley, Hubbard, and Walz, this rule demonstrated that a 4% initial withdrawal rate sustained portfolios with substantial equity holdings across most historical 30-year periods. On a $1,000,000 portfolio, 4% equates to $40,000 in year one, or $3,333.33 per month.

faqs.question: How does inflation affect retirement savings?
faqs.answer: Inflation decreases the purchasing power of your money over time, requiring you to withdraw larger dollar amounts each year to buy the same volume of goods and services. Durations are calculated using real returns, which measure investment growth after subtracting inflation. A portfolio earning 7% nominal returns alongside 3% inflation delivers an effective real return of roughly 3.9%.

faqs.question: How long does $1 million last after 60?
faqs.answer: At a 4% real return, $1,000,000 supports up to $4,774.15 a month for 30 years (age 60 to 90); at 2% real $3,696.19 and at 0% $2,777.78. Spending more than those amounts will cause the balance to run out before age 90 unless supplemented by other income.

faqs.question: How much does the real return change how long $1 million lasts?
faqs.answer: At a flat spending rate of $4,000 a month, $1,000,000 lasts 20.8 years at a 0% real return, 27.0 years at a 2% real return, and 44.9 years at a 4% real return.

faqs.question: How long will $1 million last with Social Security?
faqs.answer: Calculations count no other income, but every dollar received from Social Security lowers the monthly withdrawal required from investments. For example, if outside income reduces your monthly portfolio draw from $5,000 to $3,000, your savings last longer. At a 2% real return, pulling $3,000 a month from $1,000,000 lasts 40.6 years instead of the 20.3 years it would last if pulling the full $5,000.
